summary: This informational memo suggests ways to measure how quickly a single OSPF router's control plane converges after a change. It focuses on that one router and does not address forwarding plane performance.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4061 is a set of instructions for measuring how quickly a router running OSPF reacts to a change in the network. The point is that the test has to be identical on every router being compared: the same topology, the same steps, the same clock readings. It then defines what to measure, when to start the clock, and when to stop it.

questions: ospf single router control plane convergence
how to measure spf computation time
how do you measure ospf convergence time
what is the difference between black box and white box ospf testing
subtitle: A repeatable way to measure how quickly one router's OSPF process reacts to a change.

tldr.problem: People wanted to compare how quickly different vendors' routers converge after a network change, but the way a test is set up changes the answer, so two results could not be compared at all.
tldr.mechanism: The memo fixes the framework: four reference topologies, a set of named measurements such as dupLSAprocTime and totalSPFtime, and a list of specific steps for each test, so that the same steps are run on every implementation.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo about measurement, not about the protocol. It restricts itself to the control plane of a single router and leaves the forwarding plane, inter-area routes and external routes to other documents.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: Vishwas Manral, Russ White and Aman Shaikh

today: RFC 4061 is an Informational memo published in April 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It provides the test framework and the test procedures; the terminology it uses is set out in RFC 4062 and the caveats in RFC 4063.

sections.title: Why the Framework Matters
sections.content:
There is a growing interest in routing protocol convergence testing, with many people looking at various tests to determine how long it takes for a network to converge after various conditions occur. The major problem with this sort of testing is that the framework of the tests has a major impact on the results. Deciding when a network is considered converged, deciding what parts of the router's operation are inside the test, and other such choices have a major impact on the apparent performance that a routing protocol provides.

RFC 4061 attempts to provide a framework for OSPF performance testing, and to provide some tests for measuring some aspects of OSPF performance. The motivation is to give the user a set of tests that can produce comparable data from various vendors, with which to evaluate OSPF protocol performance on the devices.

The memo is careful about its own wording. The RFC 2119 key words are used to ensure methodological control, which the memo says is very important in the specification of benchmarks, and it says it does not specify a network-related protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Timing a router is easy to do badly. If two people time the same change but one of them stops the clock at a different moment, the numbers mean nothing to each other. This memo fixes the clock rules so that the numbers can be compared.

sections.title: What Is and Is Not Measured
sections.content:
Although the memo describes a specific set of tests aimed at characterizing the single router control plane convergence performance of OSPF processes in routers or other boxes that incorporate OSPF functionality, a key objective is to propose methodologies that produce directly comparable convergence-related measurements.

Two things are outside its scope. The first is the interaction of convergence and forwarding, because testing is restricted to events occurring within the control plane. Forwarding performance is the primary focus of RFC 2544, and it is expected to be dealt with in work that follows from RFC 3222. The second is inter-area route generation, AS-external route generation, and simultaneous traffic on the control and data paths within the device under test. Although the tests measure SPF time, flooding times and other aspects of OSPF convergence performance, the memo does not provide tests for measuring external or summary route generation, route translation, or other OSPF inter-area and external routing performance. Those areas are expected to be dealt with in a later document.

The memo also says the tests should be run more than once, since a single test run cannot be relied on to produce statistically sound results, and that the number of test runs and any variations between the tests should be recorded in the test results, with RFC 4062 saying what items should be recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything here happens inside the routing process on one router. How fast the router forwards packets afterwards is a separate question, and so are routes that come from outside the area. The memo also insists that a test be repeated, because one run is not a measurement.

sections.title: The Reference Topologies
sections.content:
Four reference topologies are used throughout the tests, and they are gathered into one section to avoid repetition.

Reference Topology 1 is the emulated topology, a simple back-to-back configuration in which the device under test is connected to a generator. The link between the generator and the device under test is assumed to be a point-to-point link, while the connections within the generator represent some emulated topology.

Reference Topology 2 is the generator and collector arrangement, in which a collector is connected to the device under test, the device under test is connected to a generator, and the generator is connected to an emulated topology. All routers are connected through point-to-point links, and the cost of all links is assumed to be the same unless otherwise noted.

Reference Topology 3 is a broadcast network, in which the device under test and a number of other routers, labelled R1 and R2 in the diagram, sit on a common broadcast link. Any number of routers could be included on the common broadcast network.

Reference Topology 4 uses parallel links, in which the device under test reaches the generator over two separate links, and the generator in turn reaches an emulated topology.

In all cases the tests and topologies are designed to allow performance measurements to be taken all on a single device, whether that is the device under test or some other device in the network. This eliminates the need for synchronized clocks within the test networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bench layouts are used, and they are drawn so that every measurement can be taken at one end. That matters, because if two machines had to be compared, their clocks would have to agree exactly.

sections.title: The Three Basic Measurements
sections.content:
The basic tests measure three aspects of the OSPF implementation as a process on the device under test: the time required to process an LSA, the flooding time, and the Shortest Path First computation.

Time required to process an LSA. Using the emulated topology, the test begins with all links up and a full adjacency established between the device under test and the generator. The memo warns that the generator has no direct knowledge of the state of the adjacency on the device under test: the adjacency may be in the Full state on the generator and the device under test may still be requesting LSAs from it, and that processing will affect the results. The generator should either wait until it sees the device under test's router-LSA listing the adjacency with the generator, or introduce a configurable delay before starting the test. The test then sends an LSA that is already in the device under test, a duplicate LSA, and notes the time between sending it and receiving the acknowledgement. That is the time taken to propagate the LSA and the acknowledgement, plus the processing time of the duplicate LSA, and it is called dupLSAprocTime. The test then sends a new LSA from the generator to the device under test, followed immediately by a duplicate LSA, meaning one that already resides in the database of the device under test but is not the same as the one just sent. The device under test acknowledges the second LSA immediately, and the time of that acknowledgement is newLSAprocTime. The time required to process the new LSA is computed by subtracting dupLSAprocTime from newLSAprocTime. The duplicate LSA cannot be the same as the one just sent, because of the MinLSInterval restriction. The memo notes that this time may or may not include the time required for flooding-related operations, depending on whether the implementation sends the acknowledgement before it floods the LSA further, after it does, or somewhere in between, so the measurement may not mean the same thing in all implementations.

Flooding time. Using the generator and collector topology, OSPF is enabled on all links and the devices are allowed to build full adjacencies. The collector is configured to block all flooding toward the device under test, while continuing to receive advertisements from it. A new set of LSAs is injected from the generator toward the collector and the device under test. On the collector, the memo asks for the time the flooding is complete across the link to the generator, and the time it is complete across the link from the device under test. The time from when the last LSA is received on the collector from the generator to when the last LSA is received on the collector from the device under test is the measurement. The memo explains why it matters: in link state protocols the loop-free nature of the network relies on the speed at which revised topology information is flooded. Depending on the number of LSAs flooded, their sizes, the number of LSUs and the rate of flooding, these numbers could vary by some amount, and the settings and variances should be reported with the test results.

SPF computation time. The test again uses the emulated topology, beginning with the device under test and the generator fully adjacent, and the default SPF timer on the device under test set to 0, so that any new LSA arriving immediately results in an SPF calculation. The generator injects a set of LSAs toward the device under test, which is allowed to converge and install all best paths in the local routing table. The duplicate LSA is sent again to establish dupLSAprocTime. The link cost between the generator and the emulated network it is advertising is then changed, and the new LSA is transmitted to the device under test, immediately followed by another LSA that duplicates one the generator has injected before, preferably a stub network somewhere within the emulated network. The generator has to make sure that outbound LSA packing is not performed for the duplicate LSAs, and that they are always sent in a separate Link-state Update packet, because if the LSA carrying the topology change and the duplicate LSA are in the same packet, the SPF starts after the duplicate LSA is acknowledged. The time between transmitting the second, duplicate, LSA and the acknowledgement for that LSA is totalSPFtime, and the total time required to run SPF is computed by subtracting dupLSAprocTime from it.

The accuracy of that test depends crucially on the time between the transmissions of the first and second LSAs. If too much time elapses, the test is meaningless, because the SPF run will complete before the second LSA is received. If less time elapses, both LSAs are handled before the SPF run is scheduled and started, and the measurement would only be for the handling of the duplicate LSA. The memo also notes that the test may not be accurate on systems that implement OSPF as a multithreaded process, where flooding takes place in a separate process, or on a different processor, from the shortest path first computations.

It is also possible to measure the SPF time with white box tests, using output supplied by the OSPF software implementer: establish a full adjacency, inject a set of LSAs and allow the device under test to stabilize and install all best paths, then change the link cost so that a full SPF is required to run although only one piece of information has changed, and measure the time required to compute a new shortest path tree, using the available show and debug information. Several caveats MUST be mentioned when this method is used. Such tests are only applicable when testing various versions or variations within a single implementation, and the same set of commands MUST be used in each iteration to ensure consistent results. The memo notes that the SPF times reported by white box and black box testing are related, and that each can be used as a sanity check on the other by comparing results, with further discussion in RFC 4063.
sections.plainLanguage: The three measurements are: how long the router takes to absorb a new routing update, how long that update takes to reach everyone else, and how long the router takes to work out new paths. The trick throughout is to send a second, known update straight afterwards, so that the time to acknowledge it gives a baseline that can be subtracted from the total.

sections.title: The Intra-Area Tests
sections.content:
The intra-area tests measure the performance of an OSPF implementation for basic tasks inside an area: forming adjacencies on a point-to-point link during initialization, forming adjacencies on point-to-point links, forming adjacencies with information already in the database, initial convergence time on a designated router electing broadcast network, link down with layer two detection, link down with layer three detection, and designated router election time on a broadcast network.

Forming adjacencies on a point-to-point link (initialization) measures the time required to form an OSPF adjacency from the time a layer two, that is data link, connection is formed between two devices running OSPF. Using the emulated topology, the test begins with the link between the generator and the device under test disabled on the device under test, with OSPF configured and operating on both devices. A set of LSAs is injected from the generator toward the device under test, the link is brought up at the device under test while the time of link carrier establishment is noted on the generator, and the time of the acknowledgement for the last LSA transmitted from the device under test is noted on the generator. The time between the carrier establishment and that acknowledgement is the total time required for the OSPF process to react to a link up event with the set of LSAs injected, including the time for the operating system to notify the OSPF process. The acknowledgement for the last LSA transmitted is used rather than the last acknowledgement received, in order to prevent timing skews from retransmitted acknowledgements or LSAs.

Forming adjacencies on point-to-point links measures the time from the first communication between two devices running OSPF. The device under test is configured so that OSPF is initialized but not running on the point-to-point link toward the generator, and OSPF is then enabled on that interface. The time of the first hello received from the device under test on the generator is noted, along with the time of the acknowledgement from the device under test for the last LSA transmitted on the generator. The time between the two is the total time required to build a FULL neighbour adjacency with the set of LSAs injected.

Forming adjacencies with information already in the database uses the generator and collector topology, with all three devices running OSPF and the link between the device under test and the generator disabled. A set of LSAs is injected into the network from the generator, and the device under test receives them through normal flooding from the collector. The link is then enabled, and the times of the first hello received from the device under test, the last DBD, that is Database Description, received on the generator, and the acknowledgement from the device under test for the last LSA transmitted are noted. The time between the hello and the acknowledgement is the total time required to build a FULL neighbour adjacency. In this test the device under test is already aware of the entire network topology, so the time measured should only include the processing of DBDs exchanged while in EXCHANGE state, the time to build a new router LSA containing the new connection information, and the time to flood and acknowledge that new router LSA.

Designated router election time on a broadcast network uses the broadcast network topology, with R1 configured as the designated router on the link and the device under test as the backup designated router. OSPF is enabled on the common broadcast link on all routers, and then the broadcast link on R1 is disabled. The time of the last hello received from R1 on R2 is noted, along with the time of the first network LSA generated by the device under test as received on R2. The time between them is the amount of time required for the device under test to complete a designated router election computation. This test includes the dead interval timer at the device under test, so the time may be factored out, or the hello and dead intervals may be reduced to lessen their impact. All changed timers, the number of routers connected to the link and other variable factors should be noted in the test results. If R1 sends a goodbye hello, typically a hello with its neighbour list empty, as it shuts its interface down, using the time when that hello is received gives a more accurate measurement.

Initial convergence time on a broadcast network, test 1 uses the broadcast network topology, beginning with the device under test connected with OSPF enabled and OSPF enabled on R1 but the broadcast link disabled. The broadcast link between R1 and the device under test is enabled, the time of the first hello received by R1 is noted, and the time when the first network LSA is flooded by the device under test at R1 is noted. The difference between the two is the time required by the device under test to converge on this new topology. The test assumes the device under test will be the designated router, and a similar test could be designed for the case where it is not. The time required to elect a designated router, as measured in the previous test, may be subtracted to give just the convergence time across a broadcast network. Unlike all the other tests, this one may not include route calculation time, because the initial route calculation may occur after the first network LSA is flooded. Test 2 uses the same setup, but takes the time of the first hello transmitted by the device under test with a designated router listed, rather than the hello received on R1, and the difference between that and the first network LSA is the period required by the device under test to converge on the new topology.

Link down with layer two detection uses the parallel links topology, beginning with OSPF in the Full state between the generator and the device under test, with both links point-to-point and able to notify the operating system immediately on link failure. Link 1 is disabled in such a way that the keepalive timers at the data link layer have no impact on the device under test recognizing the failure, for example by disconnecting the cable at the generator end or shutting the link down. The time of the link failure on the generator is noted, and then the time of receipt on the generator of the new router LSA from the device under test notifying it of the link 2 failure. The difference is the time required for an OSPF implementation to recognize and process a link failure, including the time to generate and flood an LSA describing the link down event to an adjacent neighbour. Link down with layer three detection uses the same topology, but instead disables OSPF processing on link 1 from the generator, in such a way that it does not affect link status, so the device under test MUST note the failure of the adjacency through the dead interval. The same two timestamps are then taken, and the difference is the time required to recognize and process an adjacency failure.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the day-to-day events: a link comes up, a link goes down, a neighbour is elected on a shared network. Each test says exactly which two timestamps to take and what the gap between them means. The last pair is the interesting one: a cable pulled is noticed at once, while a silent neighbour is only noticed when its dead interval expires.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states in one line that it does not modify the underlying security considerations in RFC 2328.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes how OSPF authenticates itself, so the rules in RFC 2328 still apply.

items.title: dupLSAprocTime
items.text: The time between sending a duplicate LSA and receiving its acknowledgement. It covers propagation, the acknowledgement and the processing of the duplicate, and it is the baseline subtracted from the other measurements.

items.title: newLSAprocTime
items.text: The time of the acknowledgement of a second LSA, sent immediately after a new one. Subtracting dupLSAprocTime from it gives the time to process the new LSA.

items.title: totalSPFtime
items.text: The time between transmitting a duplicate LSA and receiving its acknowledgement, after a link cost change. Subtracting dupLSAprocTime from it gives the time to run SPF.

items.title: Flooding time
items.text: The time from when the last LSA reaches the collector from the generator to when the last LSA reaches the collector from the device under test.
